title: Pip and the Locked Doors
source_title: Hackers used agentic AI in a supply chain attack on ConnectWise
full_text: Microsoft disclosed on October 21, 2026, that China state-aligned actor Storm-0940 compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup, a supply chain attack. The group used ARTEX, an agentic AI penetration testing framework. Microsoft says the actor used ARTEX to automate scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse against hundreds of organizations since September 2026. From October 10 to 14, the campaign targeted 327 accounts across eight organizations. Microsoft recorded over 151,000 failed logons, peaking at 2,900 per minute on October 11. On October 15, the AI agents gained control of several ConnectWise cloud application identities and used them to access customer environments. Wiz reported sessions lasting 24 to 30 hours and new IP addresses appearing within minutes when others were blocked. ConnectWise temporarily shut down services and is restoring them in phases over several days.

parent_card.ai_concept: Bad actors can use AI too, so people and companies need good digital locks.
parent_card.background: Microsoft said a hacker group used an AI agent to guess passwords very fast and break into a backup service called ConnectWise Cloud Backup.
parent_card.question_to_ask: Why do you think we keep our passwords secret?
parent_card.honest_answer: Some people try to break into computers. Strong, secret passwords and good security teams help keep our things safe.

key_facts: Microsoft said hackers used an AI agent in an attack.
The AI tried to guess passwords very fast.
ConnectWise turned off some services to stay safe.

hidden_elements.fun_fact: Passwords work like locks on computer doors. Long, secret passwords are harder to guess.
In the real news, the sneaky ones were hackers who used an AI tool to guess passwords very fast.
Microsoft found the attack and shared the news in October 2026.
